title: Distributed Coordination & Consistency: Quick Revision
summary: Night-before revision notes on distributed transactions and coordination: two-phase commit, sagas, the transactional outbox, exactly-once myths, leader election and Raft, distributed locks with fencing tokens, and the roles of ZooKeeper and etcd.

chapters.title: Distributed Transactions and Two-Phase Commit
points: Problem: one logical operation spans several databases or services, and it must commit everywhere or nowhere (atomic commit)
2PC phase 1 (prepare/vote): the coordinator asks every participant to prepare; each durably logs its vote, then replies YES or NO, and a YES is a promise it can still commit
2PC phase 2 (decide): all YES gives COMMIT, any NO or timeout gives ABORT; the coordinator logs the decision before sending it, and participants ack
Blocking failure: if the coordinator crashes after participants voted YES, they hold locks and cannot decide alone until it recovers (in-doubt state)
2PC vs 3PC and consensus: 3PC adds a pre-commit phase to reduce blocking but still breaks under network partitions; real systems make the coordinator fault-tolerant with Paxos or Raft

chapters.title: Sagas and the Transactional Outbox
points: Saga: a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it semantically (refund, cancel reservation), with no global lock
Orchestration: a central orchestrator tells each service what to do next and tracks state; easy to follow and debug, but risks a central coupling point
Choreography: services react to each other's events with no central controller; loosely coupled, but the flow is hard to trace and cyclic dependencies creep in
Saga caveats: sagas give no isolation (others can see intermediate state), so use semantic locks or pending states; steps and compensations must be idempotent and retryable

Transactional outbox: write the business row and an outbox row in the same local DB transaction, then a relay (poller or CDC such as Debezium) publishes to the broker, which fixes the dual-write problem and gives at-least-once delivery

chapters.title: Exactly-Once Myths and Idempotency
points: Delivery guarantees: at-most-once (may lose), at-least-once (may duplicate), exactly-once delivery is impossible over an unreliable network (Two Generals)
Practical goal is exactly-once processing (effectively-once) = at-least-once delivery + idempotent consumer
Idempotency key: the client sends a unique request ID, and the server stores the ID with the result and returns the stored result on a retry
Consumer-side dedup: record processed message IDs in the same DB transaction as the side effect, or use a unique constraint or upsert so a replay is a no-op
Kafka 'exactly-once' (idempotent producer + transactions) holds only inside Kafka read-process-write; external side effects such as emails or HTTP calls still need idempotency

chapters.title: Leader Election and Raft Basics
points: Leader election: the cluster picks one node to coordinate writes, and the safety property is at most one leader per term or epoch

Raft roles and terms: follower, candidate, leader; time is split into numbered terms, and a follower that hears no heartbeat before a randomized election timeout becomes a candidate and requests votes
Election rule: a node needs a majority quorum (N/2+1) and each node votes once per term, so a 5-node cluster tolerates 2 failures and a 3-node cluster tolerates 1; use odd sizes
Log replication: the leader appends client writes to its log, replicates via AppendEntries, and commits once a majority has stored the entry; a candidate with a less up-to-date log cannot win
Split brain: a partitioned old leader may still think it leads, but it cannot commit without a majority, and a higher term makes it step down

chapters.title: Distributed Locks, Fencing Tokens, ZooKeeper and etcd
points: Lease-based lock: the lock expires after a TTL so a crashed holder cannot block others forever; Redis SET key val NX PX ttl is the usual single-node form
Why TTL locks break: a GC pause or slow network lets the lease expire while the client still thinks it holds the lock, so two holders write at once
Fencing token: the lock service returns a monotonically increasing number with each grant, and the storage layer rejects any write carrying a token lower than the highest it has seen

ZooKeeper (ZAB consensus): znodes, ephemeral nodes that vanish with the session, sequential nodes, and watches; the lock recipe uses the lowest sequential ephemeral node, and the zxid or node version can serve as a fencing token

etcd (Raft): a key-value store with leases, watches, and revision numbers (usable as fencing tokens) used for Kubernetes state, config and election; both ZooKeeper and etcd are for small, critical coordination data, not bulk storage

chapters.title: Distributed Coordination Cheat Sheet
points: Atomic commit: 2PC = prepare/vote then commit/abort, blocks if the coordinator dies; Saga = local transactions + compensations, eventual consistency, no isolation
Saga style choice: orchestration for complex flows needing visibility; choreography for few steps and loose coupling
Reliable messaging: outbox (same-transaction write + relay) for publishing; idempotent consumer for receiving; effectively-once = at-least-once + dedup
Consensus: majority quorum N/2+1, odd cluster size, Raft term + randomized timeout elects one leader per term
Locks: always use a lease plus fencing token checked by the resource; ZooKeeper (ephemeral + sequential nodes) and etcd (leases + revisions) provide the primitives
